title: Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a single reconstructive episode that replaces a large missing segment of a human tibia or femur with living bone that has a functioning blood supply, joins the remaining bone at both ends, bears load and continues to remodel. The intended result includes the strong outer cortex and internal medullary architecture of a long bone. It would avoid donor-bone harvest and prolonged mechanical transport of bone across the gap. These are proposed capabilities, not demonstrated achievements established by the supplied evidence.

Critical-sized long-bone defects are an established reconstructive challenge. A 2023 comparative review identifies autologous bone grafting, free vascularized bone transfer, bone transport and the induced-membrane, or Masquelet, technique among the main treatments. This clinical landscape motivates the proposal, but the reviewed abstract does not establish that every human reconstruction depends on those options or that engineered grafts have comprehensively failed to match them.

Proposed scope: the defining advance is the biological and functional outcome, rather than a particular manufacturing method. A graft, an in situ regenerate, or tissue printed or assembled during surgery could qualify if it meets the same requirements. A permanent load-bearing scaffold with partial bone ingrowth would fall outside this proposed definition because it would not demonstrate replacement of the missing segment by living, remodelable bone. This boundary does not imply that such scaffold-supported reconstructions lack clinical value.

significance.text: Conditional significance: reproducible restoration of a large long-bone segment in one reconstructive episode would add a major orthopedic capability. Avoiding donor-bone harvest and prolonged transport would follow directly from the proposed success criteria. Achieving union and unprotected weight bearing within the proposed six-month window would demonstrate a clinically consequential combination of tissue formation, integration and structural function.

Potential downstream benefits include shorter disability and broader access to limb salvage, but neither follows automatically from producing living bone. Shorter disability would require comparison with existing treatment pathways, including rehabilitation and complications. Broader access would depend on cost, manufacturing reliability, surgical expertise, infrastructure and availability. The supplied evidence does not substantiate the earlier assertions about treatment failure frequency, limb-loss risk or the typical burden and duration of each established treatment.

Interpretive analogy: the advance could resemble a sharp reduction in the time and resources needed to obtain a structural material, except that the product would be living tissue capable of biological adaptation. This analogy expresses the proposed scale of the capability; it is not evidence of an economic saving or a particular reduction in treatment time. The six-month endpoint also should not be equated with a typical fracture-healing timetable without an appropriate clinical comparison.

Limits of the proposed impact: success over a specified range of defect sizes would establish that demonstrated range, not restoration at arbitrary clinical length. Pediatric use would require additional evidence of appropriate growth and development. Accelerating union of an ordinary fracture is a separate capability: it does not demonstrate replacement of an absent segment with vascularized, structurally integrated bone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is coordinated restoration of blood supply, living bone, host integration and load-bearing function across a large human segmental defect within one reconstructive episode. The supplied evidence does not establish whether a solution meeting all these requirements exists as of 1 November 2026. It therefore supports defining the capability to be demonstrated, but not an exhaustive claim that contemporary engineered grafts cannot achieve it.

Engineering synthesis: a thick construct would need circulation sufficient to sustain its living tissue throughout the defect and maintain that circulation as the tissue develops and remodels. The original research identifies durable vascularization as a central concern. However, the reviewed evidence does not establish that inadequate circulation is the principal cause of engineered-graft limitations, nor does it validate a particular vascularization mechanism. The necessary breakthrough could involve several coupled capabilities rather than one missing vascular step.

Engineering synthesis: forming bone inside a defect is only part of the task. The reconstruction must unite at both host interfaces, develop load-bearing cortical structure and medullary organization, and remain mechanically reliable while remodeling. A solution must also reconcile early structural support with eventual biological load bearing. Bridging on imaging or bone occupying part of a scaffold would not, by itself, establish all these functions.

Proposed translational barriers include consistent performance across human defect geometry and tissue conditions, a reproducible preparation or manufacturing process, and durable function after rehabilitation. Previously infected defects require a clearly defined infection-control pathway before reconstruction. Pediatric growth adds a further biological requirement beyond restoring an adult shaft segment. These are requirements inferred from the intended clinical use, not experimentally established explanations of failure in the supplied studies.

current_state.text: Allesina and colleagues’ comparative meta-analysis included six observational studies involving 364 patients treated with bone transport or the Masquelet technique. Most outcomes were broadly comparable. Excellent or good ASAMI bone outcomes were reported in 82.8% after transport and 64% after Masquelet. The authors cautioned that the evidence had a high risk of bias, so these percentages should not be treated as a definitive comparative efficacy estimate. The article appeared in Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery 143:7081–7096, online on 11 September 2023, doi:10.1007/s00402-023-05049-9. These findings were supported by the PubMed abstract described in the supplied review; the full article was not available in that review.

The supplied research attributes to Shen and colleagues a ranking of vascularized bone grafting and bone transport above bone tissue engineering, with transport ranked highest for defects longer than 8 cm and tissue engineering receiving the worst complication ranking. It identifies the publication as International Journal of Surgery 111:3030–3039, dated 1 April 2025, doi:10.1097/JS9.0000000000002283. The retained copy described in the review contained only an access challenge, without scientific text or identifying bibliographic content. Consequently, the article identity, publication details, rankings and subgroup interpretation remain unverified within this evidence set; the access limitation does not show that the reported findings are false.

The supplied research reports that Svitina and colleagues used human endothelialized callus organoids in 5 mm mouse tibial defects, with complete bridging in 3 of 4 animals in one group at four weeks. It identifies Cell Stem Cell 33:1658–1675, dated 1 October 2026, doi:10.1016/j.stem.2026.08.005. The retained copy described in the review contained only an access challenge, so the study identity, date, model and numerical outcome could not be verified. Even if confirmed, this would demonstrate a small-animal result within its tested conditions, rather than restoration of a large human load-bearing segment or achievement of the proposed clinical endpoints.

An additional report in the supplied research describes reconstruction of 6 cm sheep mandibular defects using a permanent polymer scaffold, with bone occupying 11% to 38% of scaffold volume. It gives a publication date of 24 October 2025 and identifies Nature Communications 16:9422, doi:10.1038/s41467-025-64466-z; the author byline was not captured. No retained source text or source URL was supplied for this study, leaving its details unverified here. If accurate, a mandibular reconstruction with partial bone fill in a permanent scaffold would remain distinct from biological replacement of a human tibial or femoral segment.

The supplied evidence establishes a dated clinical comparison of existing treatments and preserves several later experimental or comparative reports that require source confirmation. It does not establish the complete clinical or experimental state through 1 November 2026: the freshness record is empty, two retained sources lack article content, and the sheep source is absent. There is therefore no basis here either to declare the proposed innovation achieved or to conclude exhaustively that living human segmental reconstruction still comes only from transport, membrane grafting or vascularized donor bone.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: restore tibial or femoral defects longer than 8 cm, including an explicitly defined group with previous infection after infection control, using a single reconstructive episode without donor-bone harvest or external bone transport. The reconstruction should unite at both host junctions and permit unprotected weight bearing by six months. The 8 cm and six-month thresholds are proposed benchmarks for this concept, not established standards, validated cutoffs or claims of demonstrated feasibility.
completion_criteria.label: Defects over 8 cm unite with unprotected weight-bearing by six months

completion_criteria.text: Proposed biological and structural demonstration: document a functioning blood supply and living bone across the reconstructed segment, together with serial remodeling toward cortical and medullary architecture. Assess junctional union, mechanical function and continued biological integrity using predefined methods. Imaging evidence of bridging should be interpreted alongside function and evidence of vascularized tissue; it should not alone establish complete restoration.
completion_criteria.label: Vascularized living bone remodels toward cortical and medullary architecture

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility standard: demonstrate consistent outcomes in a prospectively defined human cohort with independent assessment and replication across clinical settings. Report defect size, anatomical site, prior infection, surrounding tissue condition, rehabilitation, complications and additional procedures. Comparative evidence would be needed to establish reductions in disability, treatment burden or cost, rather than inferring those benefits from tissue formation alone.
completion_criteria.label: Human cohort outcomes replicate across clinical settings with independent assessment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: define single episode as the definitive reconstruction after infection control, and specify which preparatory procedures, fixation measures and later interventions are compatible with that definition. Establish follow-up sufficient to assess sustained loading, remodeling, fracture, recurrent infection and revision. Temporary fixation need not be excluded, but a permanent load-bearing cage with partial bone ingrowth would not satisfy this concept’s biological replacement criterion. Acceptable complication rates and assessment schedules remain to be specified.
completion_criteria.label: Define single-episode reconstruction boundaries and follow-up for sustained biological replacement

completion_criteria.text: A 5 mm mouse defect, an intraoperative print without demonstrated living load-bearing bone, or partial scaffold ingrowth would be an intermediate result rather than completion. Demonstrations across finite defect lengths and patient groups would establish the breadth actually tested, not literal universality. Longer defects, different clinical conditions and growing children would require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Report tested defect lengths and patient groups without claiming universality

related_concepts.text: Conceptual relationship to ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb: segmental bone restoration could supply one component of whole-limb regeneration. ORT-01 additionally requires coordinated reconstruction of multiple tissues and their functional connections; a restored bone shaft would not establish regeneration of a limb.

Conceptual relationship to ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint, and ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ: all seek durable biological restoration under mechanical load. Their anatomical and functional targets differ. Restoring a long-bone segment does not establish reconstruction of a synovial joint or a functioning intervertebral disc.

Conceptual relationship to ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction: infection control could enable or protect segmental reconstruction. ORT-10’s proposed previously infected cohort assumes infection has already been controlled; it does not demonstrate eradication of mature biofilm while retaining an existing reconstruction.

Conceptual relationship to ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis: both require tissue integration capable of transmitting force. ORT-10 concerns bone formation and union between host bone and the replacement segment. ORT-04 concerns restoration of the specialized tendon–bone attachment, a distinct interface and biological task.

Conceptual relationship to ORT-06, Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss, and ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps: these capabilities could complement bone reconstruction in complex limb injuries. A restored skeletal segment alone does not establish muscle force or motor and sensory recovery, so successful bone restoration need not imply complete limb function.

Conceptual relationship to ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis: controlling where bone forms could help shape a segmental regenerate and its integration. ORT-10 additionally requires vascularization, structural organization, junctional union and load bearing. Conversely, successful segment replacement would not by itself demonstrate reversible control of osteogenesis.

Conceptual relationship to ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate: this is especially relevant to extending reconstruction to children. Restoration and remodeling of a shaft segment do not establish restoration of a growth plate or appropriate longitudinal growth. Adult segmental restoration and growth-plate regeneration therefore remain distinct capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved ORT-10’s identity and centered the definition on living, vascularized, remodelable segmental bone with clinical load-bearing function.
change_log.reason: The proposed capability remains coherent despite gaps in evidence for individual supporting assertions.

change_log.change: Replaced the exhaustive dependence claim about human reconstruction with the established treatment landscape.
change_log.reason: The reviewed 2023 abstract identifies main treatments but does not comprehensively exclude other approaches.

change_log.change: Retained vascularization and structural remodeling as concrete engineering concerns while labeling the causal account as synthesis.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish durable circulation as the principal barrier or validate a specific vascularization mechanism.

change_log.change: Expanded the Allesina result to include six observational studies, ASAMI outcomes, publication details, abstract-only access and high risk of bias.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the supported quantitative result while preventing overinterpretation of the percentages.

change_log.change: Preserved the Shen, Svitina and sheep reports with their dates, dimensions, rankings and numerical outcomes, explicitly identifying their evidentiary limitations.
change_log.reason: Missing article content prevents verification but does not justify deleting the reports or treating them as disproven.

change_log.change: Removed the exhaustive conclusion about available human reconstruction and qualified the present-day state.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record and incomplete source access cannot establish the full state through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Separated direct procedural consequences from possible benefits in disability, access and cost, and bounded the structural-material analogy.
change_log.reason: The latter benefits require comparative clinical and economic evidence; the analogy is interpretive.

change_log.change: Replaced arbitrary-length and typical-fracture implications with bounded proposed demonstrations and separate pediatric requirements.
change_log.reason: Finite tests establish demonstrated scope, and adult shaft restoration does not establish pediatric growth.

change_log.change: Clarified the proposed completion criteria, including reconstruction after infection control, biological assessment, reproducibility and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The review identified unresolved protocol details and emphasized that the numerical thresholds are proposals.

change_log.change: Explained relationships with every other supplied roster entry while retaining their distinct targets.
change_log.reason: Shared biological or reconstructive requirements do not make the innovations interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: Whether any clinical approach meets the complete proposed capability as of 1 November 2026 remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.
The intended Shen article’s identity, publication details, rankings and longer-than-8-cm subgroup findings require scientific source text.
The intended Svitina article’s identity, publication details, 5 mm model and 3-of-4 bridging result at four weeks require scientific source text.
The sheep study lacks retained source text, a supplied URL and a captured author byline; its scaffold permanence, 6 cm defect size and 11%–38% bone-fill measurement remain unverified.
The relative importance of vascularization, mechanical support, host integration and remodeling as limiting factors is not established.
A clinical protocol must define permissible preparatory and later procedures, vascular and mechanical assessments, follow-up duration and acceptable complications.
The feasibility and clinical value of the proposed greater-than-8-cm and six-month benchmarks require demonstration; benefits in disability, access and cost require comparative evidence.

brief.title: Replacing missing leg bone with living bone
possible: People missing more than 8 cm of shinbone or thighbone could have the gap replaced with living bone in a single reconstruction. They would avoid having bone taken from elsewhere in their body or slowly moved across the gap.

The replacement would have its own working blood supply, join the remaining bone at both ends and carry body weight. It would keep renewing its structure, forming a strong outer shell and an organised interior.
why: For people with large gaps in a leg bone, this would combine replacement, healing and restored weight bearing in one treatment pathway. The goal is a living part of the skeleton that can adapt as it carries load.

sources.showed: A review found broadly comparable outcomes for bone transport, which moves bone across a gap, and the Masquelet technique, a membrane-based grafting procedure. The studies had a high risk of bias.
sources.quote: Both the Masquelet technique and bone transport showed comparable results for the management of critical-sized bone defects of the lower limb.
sources.cited_for: Existing operations can reconstruct large gaps in leg bones.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate replacement with living bone in a single reconstruction without donor-bone harvest or bone transport.

sources.showed: A comparison of surgical treatments found no statistically clear differences in clinical outcomes. Grafts with their own blood supply ranked highest for healing, while engineered bone ranked lowest.
sources.quote: There were no significant differences in clinical outcomes among the treatments.
sources.cited_for: Comparisons with existing treatments set a clinical benchmark for engineered bone.
sources.not_established: The rankings do not prove that a particular treatment is superior or establish the proposed complete replacement capability.

sources.who: Hanna Svitina and colleagues at KU Leuven
sources.showed: Human cell clusters designed to resemble early healing tissue supported blood-vessel growth and regeneration across shinbone gaps in mice with weakened immune systems. Donor cells were progressively replaced as the tissue renewed itself.
sources.quote: Donor-derived cells actively contributed to early regeneration but were progressively replaced during remodeling
sources.cited_for: Engineered human tissue can guide blood-supply formation and bone regeneration in an animal model.
sources.not_established: A small-animal result does not establish durable replacement of a large human leg-bone segment that carries body weight.

shown: Svitina and colleagues have demonstrated regeneration guided by engineered human cell clusters in mice. This connects blood-vessel growth with bone formation and subsequent tissue renewal, but remains a small-animal demonstration.
missing: A human reconstruction must combine sustained blood supply, living bone, healing at both ends and reliable weight bearing.
The replacement must develop the outer shell and inner organisation of a long bone while continuing to renew itself.
Results must hold across clinical settings, with durable function and a reproducible preparation process.

milestones.label: Large leg-bone gaps heal and carry full weight
milestones.explanation: The gaps described above would have to heal at both ends and permit unprotected weight bearing within six months, including after controlled infection, without donor bone or external bone transport. This would establish clinical function.

milestones.label: Living bone develops its outer and inner structure
milestones.explanation: The whole replacement would have to sustain circulation and living bone while developing a strong outer shell and organised interior. This would establish biological restoration beyond a gap that merely looks bridged on a scan.

milestones.label: Human results repeat across clinical settings
milestones.explanation: A human study with patients and outcomes defined in advance would have to produce consistent results across clinical settings under independent assessment. This would establish reproducibility and reveal complications.

milestones.label: Treatment boundaries and lasting replacement are established
milestones.explanation: A protocol would have to define reconstruction after infection control, allowed supporting procedures and follow-up for loading, renewal and complications. This would distinguish lasting biological replacement from partial growth inside a permanent cage.

milestones.label: The tested lengths and patient groups are clear
milestones.explanation: Results would have to establish which gap lengths and patient groups the treatment serves. This would define its demonstrated reach, with longer gaps, different tissue conditions and growing children requiring further evidence.

uncertain: The relative importance of blood supply, mechanical support, attachment to existing bone and tissue renewal remains unresolved.
The proposed size and recovery targets still need demonstration, and acceptable complication rates and follow-up remain undefined.
Whether this approach would reduce disability or cost, or broaden access to limb-saving treatment, requires comparative evidence.

page.title: Single-stage regeneration of critical-size segmental defects in the tibial or femoral shaft
page.definition: A missing length of tibial or femoral shaft leaves a gap that cannot heal on its own. After one definitive reconstruction, living bone with its own blood supply grows across the gap, joins both ends and carries body weight without relying on a permanent structural scaffold. It forms a dense outer cortex around a marrow cavity and remodels as old bone is resorbed and new bone forms. The procedure requires neither bone harvested elsewhere in the patient nor bone transport, in which a segment of healthy bone is gradually moved into the gap.

goal.need: After trauma or cancer surgery, replacing a missing length of bone can take months. In one series of 32 tibial defects treated by bone transport over a plate, patients wore an external frame for an average of 91 days. Induced-membrane grafting requires a second operation weeks later to replace a cement spacer with graft. Regrowing bone in place could spare patients that operation and the pain of harvesting bone elsewhere. Infection can still require surgery before reconstruction.

figures.caption: Bone outcomes in the 2023 comparative meta-analysis.
figures.note: ASAMI classifies bone outcomes after limb reconstruction. These percentages are not union rates; treatment-group denominators are not given in the abstract.

statements.quote: provide full load-bearing capabilities within days, aid bone growth, and eventually dissolve into harmless by-products as normal bone grows.
statements.context: The Fracture Putty programme sought a material packed around a compound fracture.

statements.body: Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, CIRM Early Translational IV application TR4-06713
statements.quote: We propose to develop a novel approach for the treatment of such fractures without the need for a bone graft.
statements.context: The application’s Statement of Benefit to California concerns segmental bone loss after trauma or cancer. CIRM’s governing board approved the award round on August 28, 2013.

completion.title: A human long-bone segment is regenerated in one reconstruction without autologous bone harvest.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed human study demonstrates replacement of a critical-size tibial or femoral shaft defect by perfused living bone without autologous bone harvest or bone transport. Both host interfaces unite; regenerated bone supports full weight bearing without a permanent structural scaffold, surrounds a marrow cavity and shows serial bone resorption and formation. There is one definitive reconstructive operation after any required infection control. Temporary fixation is permitted; a planned second regenerative operation or rescue bone graft fails the single-stage condition.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no outside body was found to have published a combined test for this capability.
completion.basis: Searches of DARPA Fracture Putty documents, CIRM's segmental-fracture programme, ASTM F2721, FDA investigation guidance and registered tibia/femur protocols found no combined completion test. This synthesis combines regeneration and graft-avoidance goals without adding a defect-length, recovery-time, cohort-size or success-rate cutoff.

milestones.criterion: An engineered implant induces growth of host blood vessels and new bone within a small-animal segmental long-bone defect that cannot heal without treatment.

milestones.title: A large-animal segmental defect regenerates bone with properties similar to native bone.
milestones.criterion: In a skeletally mature large animal with a critical-size segmental long-bone defect, the new bone has microscopic structure, biochemical properties and mechanical properties similar to those of native bone. ASTM specifies no numerical margin for similarity.
milestones.set_by: ASTM International, F2721-09(2023), section 3.1.1, applied to its large-animal models. Its definition of regeneration supplies no numerical similarity margin.
milestones.threshold_quote: the formation of bone that has histologic, biochemical, and mechanical properties similar to that of native bone.

milestones.criterion: A tissue-engineered graft is implanted into a human segmental long-bone defect.

milestones.title: At 12 months, at least three of four cortices bridge and the patient bears full weight.
milestones.criterion: At 12 months after graft placement in a human tibial or femoral defect, radiographs in two planes show bridging of at least three of four cortices and CT shows consolidation. Clinical assessment shows mechanical stability and full weight bearing.
milestones.set_by: Heidelberg University Hospital, DRKS00013882 published protocol, Primary outcome measure and Follow-up sections; written for two-stage Masquelet treatment of 2–5 cm tibial or femoral defects.
milestones.threshold_quote: defined as cortical bridging of at least three out of four cortices

milestones.title: Contrast imaging documents perfusion of a human tibial or femoral graft at 12 weeks.
milestones.criterion: At 12 weeks after graft placement, contrast-enhanced ultrasound and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI assess blood flow within the graft. The study documents perfusion at the reconstructed site. The protocol specifies no minimum flow value.
milestones.set_by: Heidelberg University Hospital, DRKS00013882, graft-perfusion secondary endpoint and follow-up schedule for two-stage Masquelet reconstruction.
milestones.threshold_quote: After 12 weeks, patients also receive DCE-MRI to assess vitality of the graft

not_found: No clinical report was found demonstrating every element of the completion test together.
Svitina et al.'s full text could not be retrieved from Elsevier or KU Leuven, leaving the draft's 5 mm defect and three-of-four bridging figures unverified.
No outcome publication or posted results were found for DRKS00013882; its registry record was last updated on 1 August 2018.
DRKS00013882 gives defect size in cm³, whereas its published protocol uses cm; this discrepancy could not be resolved.
No orthopaedic society or funding programme statement was found disputing the feasibility or value of single-stage, graft-free segmental regeneration.

results.finding: Engineered organoid aggregates supported host vascularization and bone regeneration in critical-size mouse tibial defects. Sample size and effect size were unreported.
results.detail: The abstract gives no numerical defect size or time to regeneration.
results.quote: Following brief in vitro differentiation, macroscale aggregates of hECOs supported rapid host vascularization and regeneration of critical-size tibial defects in immunocompromised mice.

results.finding: Tissue-engineered grafts were implanted in 3 patients with tibial segmental defects.
results.quote: The concentrates were seeded onto a xenogenous bovine scaffold (Chronos®, Geistlich Pharma AG) and implanted into the bone defect.

results.finding: Tissue-engineered grafts were implanted in 2 patients with femoral segmental defects.
results.quote: The concentrates were seeded onto a xenogenous bovine scaffold (Chronos®, Geistlich Pharma AG) and implanted into the bone defect.

results.finding: Three tibial graft recipients underwent PET/CT at three months. Pooled tibia and femur graft blood flow averaged 0.097 mL/min.
results.detail: The blood-flow result is pooled across both bones. The source gives no tibia-specific flow value.

results.finding: Two femoral graft recipients underwent PET/CT at three months. Pooled tibia and femur graft blood flow averaged 0.097 mL/min.
results.detail: The blood-flow result is pooled across both bones. The source gives no femur-specific flow value.

results.finding: All 3 tibial graft recipients healed radiographically and maintained full weight bearing through 24 months.
results.detail: The tibial outcomes follow from the reported four successes and the identification of the sole failure as distal femoral.
results.quote: Full weight bearing was achieved 11.3 ± 5.0 weeks after surgery and was maintained up to 24 months of follow-up in four patients.

results.finding: Of 2 femoral graft recipients, 1 healed radiographically and maintained full weight bearing through follow-up.
results.detail: The proximal femoral outcome follows from the reported four successes and the identification of the distal femoral case as the sole failure.
results.quote: The patient with the largest defect sustained an implant failure in the distal femur and finally accomplished therapy by segmental transport.

results.finding: Tissue-engineered scaffold grafts were implanted in 7 patients with segmental tibial defects.
results.quote:
A total of ten patients were treated for a segmental bone defect median of 10.5 cm (IQR 3.25) of the femur (n = 3) or 
tibia (n = 7).

results.finding: Tissue-engineered scaffold grafts were implanted in 3 patients with segmental femoral defects.
results.detail: Two femoral grafts used PCL/TCP scaffolds. The midshaft femoral graft used a PCL-only scaffold.
results.quote:
A total of ten patients were treated for a segmental bone defect median of 10.5 cm (IQR 3.25) of the femur (n = 3) or 
tibia (n = 7).

results.finding: In the 7-patient tibial subgroup, 3 patients bore full weight without walking aids for over a year before complications.
results.detail: Patient 1 returned to full weight bearing after later debridement for osteomyelitis, outside the 12-month graft follow-up window.
results.quote:
Remarkably, four patients (pt. 3, 4, 5, 6) 
were pain-free and full weight-bearing without walking aids 
for over a year (mean 26.8 months) before complications 
occurred.

results.finding: The ethics-approved femoral graft case series included 5 consecutive patients.
results.detail: The article describes consent before enrollment but gives no first-enrollment date or explicit prospective enrollment design.
results.quote:
The institutional Human
Research Ethics Committee granted approval, and informed
consent to participate was obtained from all eligible patients
before enrolment.

results.finding: Five adults with segmental femoral defects averaging 14.0 cm received custom titanium cages packed with bone graft.
results.quote:
Patient-speciﬁc 3D printed titanium cages were used in 5 consecutive patients to reconstruct post-traumatic segmental
femoral defects.

results.finding: All 5 patients with segmental femoral defects achieved union and were fully weight bearing at latest follow-up.
results.detail: The illustrated CT was obtained at nine months. Metal artifact obscured much of the bone growth within the cage.
results.quote:
At latest follow-up all 5 were
ambulating, full weight bearing, and pain free, with 1 patient
using a cane when ambulating distances.

results.finding: Engineered grafts with host arteriovenous bundles produced vascularized bone in rat femoral defects, with 89% mean bone area in the endpoint histology cohort (n=5).
results.detail: The study tested the seeded scaffold and arteriovenous bundle together. Control defects received unseeded scaffolds without a vascular bundle.

results.finding: An engineered scaffold produced vascularized bone bridging 5.0-mm rat femoral defects. The supplied text omits the animal count.
results.quote: In vivo, it promoted complete defect bridging, vascularized bone formation, direct integration, and biomechanical restoration.

results.finding: Adult goat femoral repairs reached 100% of normal maximum bending load (n=3 tested at the final endpoint).
results.detail: The authors based the critical-size designation on prior work. The study included no untreated defect control.
results.quote: The maximum bending strength of the repaired bone defects reached to the 100% of normal femur at 18 months post-surgery.

results.finding: A prospective titanium scaffold study enrolled 10 patients overall, including six tibial shaft defects.
results.detail: The paper reports approval No. M2018174 and a December 2017 study start. It gives neither an approval date nor a first-enrollment date.
results.quote: The location of defects included five parts of femur and six parts of tibia, and their average defect distance was 12.2 cm.

results.finding: A prospective titanium scaffold study enrolled 10 patients overall, including five femoral shaft defects.
results.detail: The paper reports approval No. M2018174 and a December 2017 study start. It gives neither an approval date nor a first-enrollment date.
results.quote: The location of defects included five parts of femur and six parts of tibia, and their average defect distance was 12.2 cm.

results.finding: A 3D-printed titanium scaffold was implanted in one illustrated patient with a 6.3 cm tibial shaft defect.
results.detail: The scaffold supported host callus growth and was implanted without additional bone graft.
results.quote: After the routine preparation procedure, his tibial bone defect (6.3 cm) was also repaired by a 3D patient-specific scaffold without additional bone grafting.

results.finding: A 3D-printed titanium scaffold was implanted in one illustrated patient with a 9.5 cm femoral shaft defect.
results.detail: The scaffold supported host callus growth and was implanted without additional bone graft.
results.quote: After thorough debridement, osteotomy and spacer replacement (Fig. 2F), a critical femoral defect of 9.5 cm was repaired by a 3D printed porous scaffold without additional bone grafting.

results.finding: One illustrated tibial reconstruction had satisfactory weight-loading ability at 35 months.
results.detail: The reported loading assessment does not specify full weight bearing. The series also reported one tibial revision for varus deformity and scaffold loosening.
results.quote: At 35 months after surgery, his weight-loading ability and knee motion (bent or straight) of both legs were satisfactory (Fig. 3).

results.finding: One illustrated femoral reconstruction showed new bone growing from both ends and a stable scaffold over 30 months.
results.quote: We could observe newly formed bone formation from both ends to middle and robust scaffold location during the follow-up period of 30 months (Fig. 2G–J).

results.finding: A titanium cage with cancellous allograft and demineralized bone matrix was implanted in 2 human segmental tibial defects.
results.quote: This report describes a new technique for treatment of a segmental defect in long bones that uses a cylindrical titanium mesh cage, in combination with cancellous bone allograft and demineralized bone matrix putty (Grafton), stabilized with a statically locked intramedullary nail. Two clinical cases of tibia defects

results.finding: Both tibial cases (n=2) showed radiographic bony healing at 12 months.
results.detail: Full weight bearing was initiated immediately after surgery. The abstract gives no 12-month weight-bearing assessment.
results.quote: At the one-year follow-up, radiographically both cases demonstrated excellent limb alignment, stability, and bony healing. Immediate full weight-bearing was initiated in each case, and early limb functional recovery was achieved.

results.finding: In the unirradiated rat femoral graft group (n=10 enrolled), vessels grew into the constructs and mean bone area reached 14.16%.
results.detail: Donor-site preossification preceded transfer. The increase in bone area between the early and later unirradiated groups supports new bone formation within the recipient defect. Residual scaffold prevented microCT quantification of vessel ingrowth.
results.quote: Given the results from groups C and D, it is evident that bone formation took place not only in donor animals but also proceeded in unirradiated acceptors after transplantation.

results.finding: In 42 patients with segmental tibial defects, the implanted composite contained at least 70% autologous bone.
results.quote: Both edges of the bone defects were scraped until slight bleeding occurred, which is also known as the “pepper sign,” after which the bone grafting (artificial bone + autogenous bone) filled the gap of the defect, where autogenous bone accounted for no less than 70%.

results.finding: In 42 patients with grafted segmental tibial defects, the reported CT-based healing rate was 71%.
results.detail: The paper gives no 12-month time point for the 71% rate. Its CT threshold could include advanced bridging with residual gaps.
results.quote: According to the healing bone grade (>60%), the healing rate was 71%, as shown in Table  1 .

results.finding: The prospective Masquelet graft study included femoral defects in 30 of 60 patients.
results.detail: The grafts used harvested iliac crest bone, with ipsilateral fibula added in some cases.
results.quote:
Thirty femoral and 30 tibial cases were included in the 
present study.

results.finding: NVD003 phase 3 tibial graft trial (target n=12) reports its first 2 participants enrolled and implanted.
results.detail: The release describes graft placement after excision of diseased tibial bone. It gives no defect dimensions or explicit classification of the first participant’s defect as segmental.
results.quote: During February and March 2026, the first two patients enrolled in our pivotal phase 3 trial for the treatment of Congenital Pseudarthrosis of the Tibia (CPT) were successfully implanted with NVD003 in Belgium and the US.

results.finding: One patient received a tissue-engineered scaffold–flap graft in a 36-cm segmental tibial defect.
results.detail: At 18 months, a small distal unicortical nonunion was debrided and treated with iliac crest autograft. The patient achieved full weight bearing at 24 months.
results.quote: A 27-year-old adult male underwent reconstruction of a 36-cm near-total intercalary tibial defect secondary to osteomyelitis using the RMAV approach.

results.finding: In scaffold-treated sheep femoral defects (n = 10 assigned), regenerated bone reached about 80% of native Young’s modulus at six months.
results.detail: The study reports six nanoindentation test points per bone region. It does not specify how many sheep contributed to the six-month mechanical comparison.
results.quote:
while its Young’s modulus 
increased to 14.93 ± 1.47 GPa, about 80 % of that of natural bone 
(18.74 ± 1.82 GPa) (p < 0.01) (Fig. 7D).

results.finding: Skeletally mature sheep (n unreported) regenerated bone across a 2.5 cm tibial shaft defect with bending stress-strain curves similar to the native tibia.
results.detail: Carrier-only defects failed to bridge at 12 weeks. The reported mechanical similarity is qualitative.
results.quote: Implants with TGF-beta 1 showed complete bony bridging of the defect and stress-strain curves similar to the normal contralateral limb, while implants with the carrier alone failed to bridge the gap.

results.finding: One patient with a critical-size femoral shaft defect bore full weight without pain at 12 months, with almost complete fusion on CT.
results.detail: The intramedullary nail provided mechanical fixation. The clinical follow-up describes pain-free loading, and the radiographic narrative gives no cortex count.
results.quote: Twelve months after surgery, the patient presented with no pain under full weight bearing and the X-ray shows delicate but adequate bone formation. A CT-scan confirms almost complete bony fusion of the critical-sized defect and bone formation inside and outside the fully interconnected scaffold architecture (Fig.

results.finding: In one patient with a proximal tibial defect, CT showed union 12 months after graft placement.
results.detail: The tibial reconstruction used a staged Masquelet procedure with allograft, iliac crest autograft, and external fixation.
results.quote: In the tibia despite a significantly smaller defect, the CT scan revealed union 12 months after the second stage of MIMT.

results.finding: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound detected microperfusion in reconstructed tibial nonunion gaps at 12 weeks in a 13-patient study.
results.detail: The methods describe imaging 3 months after the last surgery, and Figure 3 specifies 12 weeks after the second step. The cohort included one- and two-stage reconstructions using autologous cancellous bone.
results.quote: In particular, results from the analysis of the parameter time to peak (TTP) 12 weeks subsequent to the second step are shown and compared between groups.

title = "Single-stage regeneration of critical-size segmental defects in the tibial or femoral shaft". Reason: The current title includes upper-limb bones and small gaps outside the entry’s completion test.

definition = "A missing length of tibial or femoral shaft leaves a gap that cannot heal on its own. After one definitive reconstruction, living bone with its own blood supply grows across the gap, joins both ends and carries body weight without relying on a permanent structural scaffold. It forms a dense outer cortex around a marrow cavity and remodels as old bone is resorbed and new bone forms. The procedure requires neither bone harvested elsewhere in the patient nor bone transport, in which a segment of healthy bone is gradually moved into the gap.". Reason: The definition needs to explain critical size and bone transport and distinguish the reconstructive operation from the bone growth that follows it.

goal.need = "After trauma or cancer surgery, replacing a missing length of bone can take months. In one series of 32 tibial defects treated by bone transport over a plate, patients wore an external frame for an average of 91 days. Induced-membrane grafting requires a second operation weeks later to replace a cement spacer with graft. Regrowing bone in place could spare patients that operation and the pain of harvesting bone elsewhere. Infection can still require surgery before reconstruction.". Reason: The existing figures count participants in reviews but do not tell patients how long treatment takes or which operations regeneration could spare them.

add statement by Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, CIRM Early Translational IV application TR4-06713, 2013: "We propose to develop a novel approach for the treatment of such fractures without the need for a bone graft.".
